briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Day 11, 18:00 CET

The post-crisis period enters its second day with the nuclear dimension fully resolved. All four nuclear powers — US, UK, France, Russia — are now at PEACETIME posture. The Belarus Nuclear Question (tactical weapons and Oreshnik IRBMs on Belarusian soil) has emerged as the dominant new crisis-within-a-crisis.

MILITARY: NATO forces transitioning to permanent garrison posture. Shield Force operational at Suwalki. Allied forces withdrawing to home bases (French brigade, Dutch 43rd, Finnish artillery). eFP battlegroups maintained at enhanced strength across all four Baltic/Polish positions. No military threats detected.

DIPLOMATIC: Geneva Process substantive negotiations underway. Russia engaging genuinely (nuclear de-escalation, gas restoration offer). Belarus nuclear ultimatum dominates headlines. China scaling back Taiwan exercises. Turkey accelerating S-400 transfer. Hungary in domestic political crisis.

ECONOMIC: Oil at $89 (dropping on de-escalation). Ruble recovering to 128/USD. European markets in cautious recovery. Reconstruction funding being mobilized: Germany EUR 25B, France-Germany industrial partnership, Czech ammunition surge. Baltic shipping fully restored.
narrative:
Day 11 marks the first full day of the post-crisis world order. In Geneva, the four-track negotiations enter their substantive phase as delegations settle into the Palais des Nations for what promises to be months of complex diplomacy. The most dramatic development comes from Moscow: Russia announces an immediate return to PEACETIME nuclear posture, verified through the US-Russia military hotline and P5 channels. The move — driven by Gerasimov's ascendant realist faction and the desperate need to stabilize the ruble — sends a powerful signal that the nuclear dimension of the crisis is truly over. Markets respond immediately: oil drops to $89, the ruble recovers slightly to 128/USD, and European indices post their strongest gains since the crisis began.

In Minsk, the Belarus transitional government issues an extraordinary ultimatum: Russia must remove all tactical nuclear weapons and Oreshnik IRBMs from Belarusian territory within 60 days. Tsikhanouskaya's government simultaneously requests Western security guarantees in exchange for denuclearization — a move that sends shockwaves through both NATO and Moscow. The 'Belarus Nuclear Question' instantly becomes the most consequential arms control issue since Ukraine's 1994 Budapest Memorandum. Washington, caught between supporting democratic Belarus and managing the terrifying logistics of nuclear weapon removal from an unstable transitional state, dispatches a senior interagency team to Minsk within hours.

NATO's post-crisis architecture continues to solidify. Poland proposes a tripartite Polish-Lithuanian-US Suwalki Garrison Command with integrated planning authority. Lithuania launches a EUR 2.1 billion reconstruction initiative. The Baltic states formally establish the Baltic Defense Council with a permanent secretariat in Riga. Germany announces a EUR 25 billion 'Marshall Plan for Eastern Europe' co-led with France. The UK extends its carrier strike group deployment and expands the JEF framework. Turkey accelerates S-400 transfer to US custody, completing ahead of the 90-day schedule.

China makes a calculated move: scaling back Taiwan Strait exercises by 60% and proposing a six-month military confidence-building period with the US. Simultaneously, Beijing launches a USD 25 billion 'Global South Reconstruction Fund' with Brazil, India, South Africa, and Egypt as co-managers — a direct challenge to Western-dominated reconstruction efforts. Hungary, with government approval at a crisis-level 22%, announces a EUR 2.5 billion domestic stimulus, judicial reforms, and releases 50 political prisoners in a desperate bid to unlock frozen EU funds and save Orban's political skin.

surprises: A leaked Kremlin document — attributed to FSB chief Bortnikov — surfaces on Telegram channels, detailing a plan to assassinate Gerasimov and blame it on Ukrainian intelligence. The document's authenticity is unverified but its publication forces Putin to publicly embrace Gerasimov's reform role, inadvertently strengthening the military realist faction. Russian state media scrambles to denounce the leak as a 'Western fabrication' while privately, Kremlin officials investigate the source.

In Kaliningrad, 3,000 residents stage the first unauthorized public protest since 2011, demanding the resignation of the regional governor and an end to militarization. 'We are civilians, not hostages,' reads the largest banner. The protest is small but symbolically devastating — Kaliningrad was supposed to be the fortress that justified the entire Suwalki operation.
